analysis.one_liner: Codifies Roe v. Wade's protections for abortion before viability and contraception access nationwide.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to restore the legal standard of Roe v. Wade never got a committee vote or floor debate before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write the core holdings of Roe v. Wade and related Supreme Court cases into federal statute after the Court overturned Roe in Dobbs. It guarantees every person the right to use contraceptives, protects a woman's choice to end a pregnancy before fetal viability, allows states to restrict abortion after viability except to protect the life or health of the woman, and lets the Justice Department or affected individuals sue states that violate it. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Women and other people who need contraception or abortion care, especially in states that have banned or sharply restricted abortion since the Dobbs decision. The bill would give them a federal legal right to sue and would let the Department of Justice enforce it. Abortion and contraceptive care providers would also gain a stable national legal standard instead of a patchwork of state laws.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People seeking contraception or abortion care

how_it_helps.text: The bill guarantees all persons the right to make certain reproductive decisions without undue government interference and bars states from prohibiting the use of contraceptives or contraceptive care.
It bars states from imposing an undue burden on a woman's choice to end a pregnancy before fetal viability, restoring the legal standard the Supreme Court used in Roe v. Wade and Casey.
It allows the Attorney General or any adversely affected person to sue in federal or state court to block state laws that violate the Act, with attorney's fees available to the winning party.

It preserves a state's ability to restrict abortion after viability, except where termination is medically indicated to protect the life or health of the pregnant woman, and leaves conscience-protection laws untouched.

analysis.who_pays: States that have enacted abortion bans or tight restrictions since Dobbs would lose those laws to federal litigation. Anti-abortion advocacy organizations would lose the state-level restrictions they have won since 2022. Taxpayers bear the cost of Department of Justice enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: States restricting abortion and anti-abortion groups

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides state abortion laws enacted by democratically elected legislatures after the Dobbs decision returned the question to them; voters in states that chose bans would see those choices displaced by federal law.

The bill would produce a wave of federal litigation over what counts as an 'undue burden' or a 'reasonable' health regulation, since it lets any affected person sue and courts would have to define those terms case by case.

It allows state regulation of abortion after viability, so it stops short of protecting abortion access in all circumstances and leaves that later-pregnancy line to medical judgment tests that courts would litigate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: a national right to contraception and to abortion before viability, enforceable in court, replacing a state-by-state patchwork where abortion is now banned in some states. The costs are real but constitutional in nature: it displaces state democratic choices on abortion and invites years of litigation over its standards. For the people most affected, the bill's protections are worth far more than the procedural objections.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Kaine introduced the bill on February 9, 2023 with Sens. Murkowski, Sinema, and Collins as original cosponsors, making it a rare bipartisan effort to restore abortion rights.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in its record for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State legislatures with abortion bans keep their laws, and anti-abortion advocacy organizations keep the state restrictions they won after Dobbs. No one gained new protection.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was genuinely bipartisan — a Democrat, two Republicans, and an independent — but because the bill never received a hearing or a vote, there is no record of where the parties stood as a whole.

industries.note: Providers would operate under a stable national standard instead of a state-by-state patchwork of bans and restrictions, and could rely on a federal right to sue. Their gain is access for the patients they serve.
A guaranteed national right to contraception protects demand for contraceptive products, which the bill's own findings describe as interstate commerce.

industries.industry: Crisis pregnancy centers and religious-objector providers
industries.note: The bill preserves conscience-protection laws, so objectors keep existing exemptions, but it forecloses state laws that would further restrict abortion access they oppose.
